question:
Patient note:
A 58-year-old man lies on the stretcher in the ambulatory procedure suite awaiting a scheduled ten-minute shave-and-curette of an enlarging seborrheic keratosis on the right posterior shoulder under local anesthesia with a small field block; the dermatologic team anticipates a single elliptical excision with placement of a few simple interrupted sutures and same-day discharge. He was transferred from the medical ward rather than walking in from home because over the past eight days the orthopedics service has kept him on strict bed-to-chair activity orders after immobilizing his left lower leg in a well-padded fiberglass cast that extends from just below the tibial tuberosity to the metatarsal heads to protect a high-grade Achilles tendon strain sustained when he slipped on wet pavement; no fracture lines were seen on plain radiographs, but weight bearing was discouraged and nursing documentation shows he has ambulated fewer than sixty assisted steps per 24-hour period since the cast was applied. Three weeks prior to today he completed a seven-day course of oral levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia documented on chest radiograph by a right middle-lobe infiltrate accompanied by a brief febrile episode to 38.3 °C; repeat imaging last week demonstrated interval clearing, and he remains afebrile with a normal white-cell count. He has not been taken to the operating room, endoscopy suite, or interventional radiology in the past month, and the present skin procedure represents his first encounter with a scalpel in more than five years. Past medical history is otherwise notable only for asymptomatic mild hyperhomocysteinemia discovered during a life-insurance physical two years ago; serum levels at that time were 19 µmol/L, and he was advised—though inconsistently complies—to take daily folate and vitamin B12 supplements. He denies any previous or current episodes of heart-failure decompensation, systemic inflammatory response, urinary infections, gastrointestinal disease, connective-tissue disorders, chronic lung pathology, or cancer. He has never experienced unilateral calf swelling, pleuritic chest pain, hemoptysis, or imaging-confirmed thromboembolic disease, and none of his first-degree relatives have required anticoagulation for idiopathic clot. Genetic screening performed at a commercial laboratory after the homocysteine result did not detect factor V Leiden or the prothrombin G20210A mutation, and a thrombophilia workup by his primary physician showed normal anticardiolipin and lupus anticoagulant panels, which were not repeated. He quit smoking fifteen years ago after a 20-pack-year exposure, drinks a glass of red wine with dinner twice a week, and denies illicit drug use. Home medications include lisinopril 10 mg daily for well-controlled hypertension, over-the-counter ibuprofen as needed for cast-related discomfort, and an OTC folic acid–B12 combination he remembers “about half the time.” He has taken no glucocorticoids, hormone therapy, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, or antiplatelet drugs. Review of systems this morning is negative for dyspnea, orthopnea, productive cough, chest tightness, palpitations, abdominal pain, or neurologic deficits. Vital signs recorded twenty minutes ago show temperature 36.7 °C, blood pressure 128/76 mm Hg, heart rate 70 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98 % on ambient air; body mass index is 28 kg/m². On examination he reclines comfortably with the head of the bed elevated to 30° while scrolling on his tablet; conjunctivae are pink, sclerae anicteric, and the oropharyngeal view is Mallampati class II. Neck veins are not distended, the point of maximal impulse is nondisplaced, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs or gallops, and lungs are clear bilaterally with full excursions. The abdomen is soft and nontender, bowel sounds are present, and no organomegaly is appreciated. Inspection of the lower extremities reveals the intact left leg cast with clean edges and no foul odor; exposed toes are warm with brisk capillary refill, and posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis pulses are palpable 2+. The contralateral limb is free of edema, varicosities, or tenderness, and calf circumferences are symmetric at 37 cm. Skin over the right posterior shoulder displays a 1.8-cm waxy, slightly verrucous plaque marked for removal; there is no regional lymphadenopathy. Neurologic screening shows intact cranial nerves and 5/5 strength in all uncasted muscle groups. Peripheral access today consists of a single 20-gauge IV cannula in the right hand running normal saline at keep-open rate; he has never had a peripherally inserted central catheter, port, or dialysis fistula. Morning laboratory work drawn through the IV line shows hemoglobin 14.0 g/dL, hematocrit 42 %, platelets 243 × 10⁹/L, leukocytes 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.96 mg/dL, AST 22 U/L, ALT 24 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 88 U/L, total bilirubin 0.8 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.1 s with an international normalized ratio 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 30 s; the chemistry lab did not repeat homocysteine today given the recent known elevation. A baseline 12-lead electrocardiogram shows normal sinus rhythm at 68 beats/min with preserved intervals and no ischemic changes, and a portable chest radiograph obtained three days ago during cough evaluation reveals clear lungs and a normal mediastinal silhouette. Sequential pneumatic compression devices are coiled at the foot of the stretcher but have not yet been applied, and per institutional policy no pharmacologic thromboprophylaxis has been administered before a purely cutaneous excision of this duration. He has been nil per os since midnight, last voided at 0600, and expresses understanding of the planned procedure as well as the expectation that he will return to the medical ward for continued non-weight-bearing care of his ankle injury immediately after recovery.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini score sums weighted perioperative VTE risk factors. The result here depends on the BMI criterion used.
- Age 58 (41–60 years) = 1.
- Planned minor surgery (10-minute skin excision) = 1.
- Pneumonia within the past month, even though now resolved = 1.
- Bed confinement for more than 72 hours (eight days of bed-to-chair activity) = 2.
- Immobilizing lower-leg cast = 2.
- Known elevated serum homocysteine = 3.
These factors sum to 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 10. This total assumes no point for BMI 28. Under the commonly used Caprini criterion of BMI >25 kg/m², BMI contributes 1 additional point, yielding 11 instead.
Final answer: 10
